title: What is Data Structures and their Types ?

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand Data Structures

Imagine you walk into a library that has one million books. But there is no catalogue, no shelves organised by genre, no alphabetical ordering. Every book is just piled in one enormous random heap. Finding any specific book would take hours. The books are all there. The information exists. But without a system to organise it, the library is essentially useless.

Now imagine the same library with books sorted alphabetically by author, grouped by genre, with a digital catalogue that tells you exactly which shelf a book is on. Finding any book takes seconds. The same million books, the same amount of information, but a completely different experience because of how the data is structured.
That is exactly what data structures do for programs. The data is not the problem. The way you organise, store, and access that data is everything.

Think about Google Maps calculating the fastest route between two cities across a road network with millions of intersections. Or a hospital database retrieving a patient’s full medical history from millions of records in milliseconds. Or a social network suggesting people you might know from a graph of a billion users and their connections. None of these applications are possible without choosing the right data structure for each problem.
is a specialised format for organising, storing, and accessing data in a computer’s memory so that operations on that data can be performed efficiently.
Different problems need different organisational approaches. A phone book is organised differently from a family tree, which is organised differently from a waiting queue at a hospital
A data structure defines how data items are arranged relative to each other and how they are laid out in memory
The arrangement of the data directly determines how fast you can find, add, remove, or update items
Without structure, finding data is slow:

# Unstructured: searching 1 million users takes up to 1 million comparisons
users = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", ..., "Zara"]   # 1,000,000 names in random order
# Finding "Zara" might require checking every single element
With the right structure, the same search is instant:

# Structured: a dictionary (hash map) finds any name in roughly 1 step
users = {"Alice": 1, "Bob": 2, "Carol": 3, ..., "Zara": 1000000}
# Finding "Zara" takes the same time regardless of list size
print(users["Zara"])   # Instant
Same data. Completely different performance. The only difference is the data structure.
These two terms are often confused but mean different things.
The kind of value a variable holds
The way multiple values are organised together
Storage format of a single value
A data type is a single container. A data structure is a system of containers with rules about how they relate to each other.
How Data Structures Work Under the Hood
This is the section most introductions skip, and it explains why the choice of data structure changes not just how code looks but how fast it runs and how much memory it uses.

Your computer’s RAM is a massive grid of storage cells, each with a unique numeric address. When your program creates any data, the operating system allocates some of these cells and your data goes in. The data structure determines how those cells are used and how they relate to each other.

Memory address:  1000  1001  1002  1003  1004  1005
Value stored:    [10]  [20]  [30]  [40]  [50]  [--]
                  ^--- Array: elements side by side in consecutive addresses

Memory address:  1000        2500        3700
Value stored:    [10 | 2500] [20 | 3700] [30 | NULL]
                  ^--- Linked list: elements scattered, each holding the address of the next

The array stores elements in consecutive memory cells. The linked list stores elements anywhere in memory and connects them with pointers. This single structural difference is why array access is O(1) (instant) but linked list access is O(n) (must follow the chain).
Time Complexity and Big O Notation
Every data structure has different performance characteristics for different operations. These are described using
, which expresses how the time taken grows as the amount of data grows.
Same speed regardless of data size
Data structures divide into two primary categories based on how elements relate to each other:
. They can also be classified by memory allocation:

, elements are arranged in a sequence. Each element has a predecessor and a successor (except the first and last). All elements exist on a single level, and you can traverse all of them in one continuous pass.
is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in
. You access any element directly using its index in O(1) time.

codes.Python:
# Python lists function as dynamic arrays
scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88]

print(scores[0])    # 85  (index access: O(1))
print(scores[2])    # 78
print(len(scores))  # 5

# Traversing an array
for score in scores:
    print(score)

# 2D array (matrix)
matrix = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9]
]
print(matrix[1][2])   # 6 (row 1, column 2)
codes.JavaScript:
let scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88];
console.log(scores[0]);      // 85
console.log(scores.length);  // 5
scores.push(76);             // Add to end: O(1)
scores.splice(2, 1);         // Remove from middle: O(n)

content.text: When you need fast random access by index, when the size of the data is known in advance, when elements are of the same type, and when cache efficiency matters (contiguous memory means fewer cache misses).

is a collection of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer (reference) to the next node. Elements are not stored in contiguous memory. They can be scattered anywhere in memory and are connected through pointers.
Node 1: [Data: 10 | Next: -->] --> Node 2: [Data: 20 | Next: -->] --> Node 3: [Data: 30 | Next: NULL]
Each node points only to the next node. Traversal in one direction only
Each node has two pointers, one to the next node and one to the previous node. Allows traversal in both directions
The last node points back to the first node, forming a circle
Time Complexity of Linked List Operations:
O(n) or O(1) with tail pointer

Use an array when you need fast index-based access and have a fixed or known size. Use a linked list when you need frequent insertions and deletions at the beginning or middle, or when the size changes frequently and you want to avoid memory reallocation.
is a linear data structure that follows the
principle. The last element added is the first one to be removed. Think of it like a stack of plates: you always add and remove from the top.

Push 10 → Stack: [10]
Push 20 → Stack: [10, 20]
Push 30 → Stack: [10, 20, 30]
Pop     → Returns 30, Stack: [10, 20]
Peek    → Returns 20 (just looks, does not remove)
Add an element to the top
Remove and return the top element
Return the top element without removing it
Check if the stack has no elements

codes.Python:
# Using a list as a stack
stack = []

stack.append(10)    # Push
stack.append(20)
stack.append(30)
print(stack)        # [10, 20, 30]

top = stack.pop()   # Pop
print(top)          # 30
print(stack)        # [10, 20]

print(stack[-1])    # Peek: 20 (does not remove)

content.text: Function call management (the call stack itself is a stack), undo/redo functionality in text editors, browser back/forward navigation, checking balanced parentheses, evaluating arithmetic expressions, and depth-first search in graphs.
is a linear data structure that follows the
principle. The first element added is the first one to be removed. It works like a queue of people at a ticket counter: the person who arrived first gets served first.

Enqueue 10 → Queue: [10]
Enqueue 20 → Queue: [10, 20]
Enqueue 30 → Queue: [10, 20, 30]
Dequeue    → Returns 10, Queue: [20, 30]
Front      → Returns 20 (just looks, does not remove)
Add an element to the rear (back)
Remove and return the element from the front
Return the front element without removing it
Check if the queue has no elements

codes.Python:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()

queue.append(10)     # Enqueue
queue.append(20)
queue.append(30)
print(queue)         # deque([10, 20, 30])

front = queue.popleft()   # Dequeue
print(front)         # 10
print(queue)         # deque([20, 30])

print(queue[0])      # Peek: 20

content.text: Basic FIFO, elements enter at rear and exit at front
The rear wraps around to the front when the end is reached, reusing empty space
Elements can be added or removed from both ends
Elements are served based on priority rather than arrival order
CPU task scheduling, print job management, handling requests on a web server, breadth-first search in graphs, simulating real-world waiting lines, and buffering data streams.
, elements are not arranged sequentially. One element can connect to multiple others. The data exists across multiple levels, and you cannot traverse all elements in a single continuous pass.
is a hierarchical non-linear data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. The topmost node is the
. Every node (except the root) has exactly one parent, but can have multiple children.

Root
         /    \\
      Node A  Node B
      /   \\       \\
   Node C Node D  Node E   ← Leaf nodes
A node with child nodes below it
A node connected below a parent
The number of edges on the longest path from root to a leaf
The number of edges from the root to a specific node
is a tree where each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

codes.Python:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

# Build a binary tree
root = TreeNode(1)
root.left = TreeNode(2)
root.right = TreeNode(3)
root.left.left = TreeNode(4)
root.left.right = TreeNode(5)

# Inorder traversal: left, root, right
def inorder(node):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder(node.left)
    print(node.value, end=" ")
    inorder(node.right)

inorder(root)   # Output: 4 2 5 1 3

content.text: is a binary tree with an ordering rule: all values in the left subtree of any node are smaller than that node, and all values in the right subtree are larger. This ordering makes searching very efficient.
: all nodes in the left subtree have values less than
, and all nodes in the right subtree have values greater than

Representing hierarchical data (file systems, organisation charts, XML/HTML documents), implementing sorted data with fast search, and anywhere you need to represent parent-child relationships between data.
is a non-linear data structure consisting of
(connections between nodes). Unlike a tree, a graph has no strict hierarchy: any node can connect to any other node, cycles are allowed, and there is no single root.
A fundamental unit of the graph
Edges have a direction (A points to B does not mean B points to A)
Edges have no direction (connection is mutual)
Each edge has a numerical weight (like distance or cost)
A sequence of vertices connected by edges
A path that starts and ends at the same vertex

Undirected graph:          Directed graph:
  A - B - C                 A --> B --> C
  |   |                     |
  D - E                     v
                            D
means there is an edge from vertex

# Adjacency matrix for 4 vertices
adjacency_matrix = [
    [0, 1, 0, 1],   # Vertex 0 connects to 1 and 3
    [1, 0, 1, 0],   # Vertex 1 connects to 0 and 2
    [0, 1, 0, 1],   # Vertex 2 connects to 1 and 3
    [1, 0, 1, 0]    # Vertex 3 connects to 0 and 2
]
Each vertex stores a list of its neighbours. More memory-efficient for sparse graphs.

# Adjacency list
graph = {
    0: [1, 3],
    1: [0, 2],
    2: [1, 3],
    3: [0, 2]
}

# Breadth-first search (BFS)
from collections import deque

def bfs(graph, start):
    visited = set()
    queue = deque([start])
    visited.add(start)

    while queue:
        vertex = queue.popleft()
        print(vertex, end=" ")
        for neighbour in graph[vertex]:
            if neighbour not in visited:
                visited.add(neighbour)
                queue.append(neighbour)

bfs(graph, 0)   # 0 1 3 2
where V = number of vertices, E = number of edges.

Social networks (friends connections), Google Maps (roads and cities), the internet (web pages and links), flight route planning, dependency resolution in software packages, recommendation systems, and any problem involving relationships between entities.
has its size fixed at the time of declaration. Memory is allocated at compile time and cannot be changed while the program runs.
Memory is allocated at compile time
Can waste memory if fewer elements are stored than capacity
Example: C-style arrays declared with a fixed size
can grow and shrink at runtime. Memory is allocated as needed during program execution.

# Python list: dynamic, grows automatically
items = []
for i in range(100):
    items.append(i)   # Grows as needed
print(len(items))     # 100

for i in range(50):
    items.pop()       # Shrinks as needed
print(len(items))     # 50
Size can change as the program runs
No wasted memory (only allocates what is needed)
Slightly slower due to dynamic allocation overhead
Examples: linked lists, Python lists, Java ArrayLists, C++ vectors
are the basic types provided directly by the programming language. They hold a single value and are the building blocks for all other structures.

age = 25           # int
price = 9.99       # float
name = "Alice"     # str
is_active = True   # bool
are built from primitive types and organise multiple values with relationships between them. These are further divided into linear and non-linear.

# Non-primitive: stores multiple related values with structure
scores = [85, 92, 78]                    # Array/List
student = {"name": "Alice", "age": 20}  # Dictionary/Hash Map
unique_tags = {"python", "coding"}       # Set
call_history = []                        # Can be used as Stack or Queue
Multiple values in hierarchy or network
Every data structure supports a set of fundamental operations. Understanding these operations and their costs is how you choose the right structure for a problem.
Visiting every element exactly once to process or print it.

# Array traversal: O(n)
scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88]
for score in scores:
    print(score)
Finding a specific element within the structure.
Adding a new element to the structure.

# Stack insertion: O(1)
stack = [10, 20, 30]
stack.append(40)   # Push to top

# Array insertion at middle: O(n)
arr = [10, 20, 40, 50]
arr.insert(2, 30)  # Insert 30 at index 2: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
Removing an element from the structure.

# Stack deletion: O(1)
stack.pop()   # Remove from top

# Array deletion: O(n) if not at end
arr.pop(2)    # Remove element at index 2
Arranging elements in a specific order.

# Python built-in sort (Timsort): O(n log n)
arr = [64, 34, 25, 12, 22]
arr.sort()
print(arr)   # [12, 22, 25, 34, 64]

# Array update: O(1)
arr[2] = 99   # Update element at index 2 instantly

codes.Python:
# Dictionary (Hash Map)
student = {"name": "Alice", "age": 20, "grade": "A"}
print(student["name"])   # Alice: O(1)

# Set
unique_numbers = {1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1}
print(unique_numbers)   # {1, 2, 3}  (duplicates removed)

# Deque (efficient queue and stack)
from collections import deque
dq = deque([1, 2, 3])
dq.appendleft(0)   # Add to front: O(1)
dq.append(4)       # Add to back: O(1)
print(dq)          # deque([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])

content.text: Data structures power every piece of software you use. Here are the specific structures that make each system work.
to determine which process runs next. Each process has a priority, and the scheduler always picks the highest-priority process. The call stack used by every program is literally a

import heapq

# Priority queue for process scheduling
# (priority, process_name)
scheduler = []
heapq.heappush(scheduler, (1, "High Priority Task"))
heapq.heappush(scheduler, (3, "Low Priority Task"))
heapq.heappush(scheduler, (2, "Medium Priority Task"))

while scheduler:
    priority, task = heapq.heappop(scheduler)
    print(f"Running:{task} (priority{priority})")

# Output:
# Running: High Priority Task (priority 1)
# Running: Medium Priority Task (priority 2)
# Running: Low Priority Task (priority 3)
Web Browsers: Back and Forward Navigation
application. Every page you visit is pushed onto the history stack. Pressing back pops from the stack. A second stack holds forward history.

back_stack = []
forward_stack = []
current_page = "google.com"

def navigate(url):
    global current_page
    back_stack.append(current_page)
    forward_stack.clear()   # Clear forward history on new navigation
    current_page = url
    print(f"Now on:{current_page}")

def go_back():
    global current_page
    if back_stack:
        forward_stack.append(current_page)
        current_page = back_stack.pop()
        print(f"Back to:{current_page}")

navigate("github.com")
navigate("stackoverflow.com")
go_back()    # Back to: github.com
go_back()    # Back to: google.com

(BFS) to discover and index pages. Starting from a known page, it finds all links on that page, adds them to the queue, visits each one, finds more links, and continues. The graph of web pages and their links is stored as a massive

codes.Python:
from collections import deque

def bfs_web_crawler(start_url, max_pages=10):
    visited = set()
    queue = deque([start_url])
    visited.add(start_url)
    page_count = 0

    while queue and page_count < max_pages:
        url = queue.popleft()
        print(f"Crawling:{url}")
        page_count += 1

        # Simulate finding links on the page
        links = get_links(url)    # Returns a list of URLs found on the page
        for link in links:
            if link not in visited:
                visited.add(link)

content.text: (specialised balanced trees) to index data. An index allows the database to find any record in O(log n) time instead of scanning every record in O(n) time. For a table with 100 million rows, the difference is finding a record in about 27 steps versus 100 million steps.
Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn model their user networks as
. Each user is a vertex, and each friendship or follow is an edge. Finding mutual friends, suggesting new connections, and computing degrees of separation are all graph algorithms.

. Folders are nodes, and files are leaf nodes. Operations like listing all files in a directory, calculating the total size of a folder, or searching for a file by name all use tree traversal recursively.
Hash Map: The O(1) Lookup Structure
(also called a dictionary or hash table) is one of the most powerful and commonly used data structures. It stores key-value pairs and provides average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion.
takes the key, performs a calculation, and produces an index. The value is stored at that index in an underlying array.

key: "Alice"
hash("Alice") → 42
Store value at index 42 in the array
again, and you jump directly to index 42. No scanning required.

is a specialised tree-based structure where the parent is always greater than (max-heap) or less than (min-heap) its children. The root is always the maximum or minimum element, allowing instant access to the extreme value.

import heapq

# Min-heap (Python's heapq is a min-heap by default)
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, 30)
heapq.heappush(heap, 10)
heapq.heappush(heap, 20)

print(heap[0])              # 10: minimum is always at index 0, O(1)
print(heapq.heappop(heap))  # 10: remove minimum, O(log n)
print(heapq.heappop(heap))  # 20
print(heapq.heappop(heap))  # 30

(prefix tree) is a tree-like structure optimised for string operations. Each node represents a character, and paths from root to leaves represent complete words. Used in autocomplete, spell checkers, and IP routing.
Every data structure involves a trade-off between memory usage and speed. Using more memory often allows faster operations.

# Time-efficient: O(1) lookup but O(n) extra memory
word_set = set(["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"])
print("apple" in word_set)   # True: O(1)

# Memory-efficient: O(1) extra memory but O(n) lookup
word_list = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]
print("apple" in word_list)  # True: O(n) - scans the whole list

For a list of 10 million words, the set lookup is millions of times faster. The cost is extra memory for the hash table. Choosing between them depends on whether memory or speed is more constrained in your application.
Advantages of Using the Right Data Structure
The right data structure dramatically reduces the time and memory required for operations. A hash map lookup is O(1) vs O(n) for a list search
Data structures provide a logical way to organise related data, making programs easier to reason about
Standard data structures (stacks, queues, trees, hash maps) are well-understood abstractions that can be reused across different parts of a program and different projects
Sorting, searching, graph traversal, and dynamic programming all depend on specific data structures. Knowing the structure enables the algorithm
A program using the right data structure scales gracefully as data grows. An O(log n) tree lookup on 1 billion records is still fast. An O(n) list scan is not
More powerful data structures (balanced trees, graphs, tries) are significantly harder to implement correctly than simple arrays or lists
Linked lists use extra memory per node for pointers. Hash maps allocate more space than needed to reduce collisions. Trees store pointers alongside data. These overheads add up at scale
Using a list where a hash map is needed, or a tree where an array suffices, can make a program orders of magnitude slower without producing any error. The code runs, but far too slowly
Linked lists, trees, and graphs store nodes scattered across memory. Accessing them causes cache misses, which are much slower than accessing contiguous array elements
Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) maintain O(log n) guarantees through rotations on every insertion and deletion. These rotations add constant overhead that a simple array never incurs
When two keys hash to the same index, the hash map must handle the collision. Poor hash functions or high load factors degrade hash map performance toward O(n)
Data structures are the organisational backbone of every piece of software ever written. Here is a recap of everything covered:
specialised format for organising and accessing data
so that operations can be performed efficiently. The same data structured differently can perform millions of times faster or slower
(array, linked list, stack, queue) store elements in a sequence.
(tree, graph) store elements in hierarchical or network relationships
provide O(1) index access but O(n) insertion/deletion in the middle.
provide O(1) insertion at the head but O(n) index access. The choice depends on which operation dominates your use case
enforce LIFO (Last In First Out) and are used for function calls, undo operations, and backtracking.
enforce FIFO (First In First Out) and are used for task scheduling, request handling, and BFS
maintains sorted order and provides O(log n) search when balanced.
grow and shrink at runtime (Python lists, linked lists)
provide average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion by using a hash function to map keys to array indices. They are the go-to structure when fast key-based access is needed
provide O(1) access to the minimum or maximum and O(log n) insertion. They power priority queues and efficient sorting

Data structures are not about memorising implementations. They are about developing an instinct for how data should be shaped for a given problem. When you see a problem involving ordered retrieval, you think queue. When you see fast lookup by key, you think hash map. When you see hierarchical relationships, you think tree. Building that instinct is what separates programs that merely work from programs that work efficiently.

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand Binary Search

Imagine you are looking for a word in a dictionary that has 1,000 pages. You could start from page 1 and flip through every single page until you find it. If the word is near the end, you might flip through 999 pages. On average, you flip through 500 pages every time you search.

Or you could open the dictionary to the middle, page 500. If the word comes alphabetically before the words on that page, you know it must be in the first half. If it comes after, you know it is in the second half. Either way, you have just eliminated 500 pages of searching in one step. Open to the middle of the remaining half. Eliminate half again. You repeat this process and find any word in roughly 10 steps, regardless of whether the dictionary has 1,000 pages or 1,000,000 pages.
That is binary search. And it is one of the most fundamental and elegant algorithms in all of computer science.

Now think bigger. A database with 1 billion records needs to find a specific user by ID. A linear scan would check up to a billion records. Binary search finds it in at most 30 comparisons. A game needs to find if a player’s score qualifies for a top-100 leaderboard. A navigation system needs to locate a GPS coordinate in a sorted spatial index. A compiler needs to look up a variable name in a symbol table. All of these use binary search or algorithms built on top of it.
Binary search is not just an interview topic. It is the foundation of database indexing, version control debugging tools, IP routing, autocomplete systems, and machine learning hyperparameter tuning.
is a searching algorithm that finds a target value within a
collection by repeatedly dividing the search space in half and discarding the half that cannot contain the target.
Its purpose is to locate a specific value within a collection of data
Binary search requires the data to be ordered. Without ordering, halving the search space tells you nothing useful
Each comparison eliminates exactly half of the remaining possibilities
Discarding the half that cannot contain the target:
Because the data is sorted, knowing the middle value’s relationship to the target immediately tells you which half is relevant
Middle index = (0 + 9) / 2 = 4. Value at index 4 is

How Binary Search Works Under the Hood
This is the section most tutorials skip, and it explains the mathematical foundation that makes binary search so remarkably fast.
Every time binary search runs one comparison, it halves the remaining search space. Starting with

After 1 comparison: n/2 elements remain
After 2 comparisons: n/4 elements remain
After 3 comparisons: n/8 elements remain
After k comparisons: n/2^k elements remain
The search ends when there is 1 element left (or 0 if not found):
This means binary search requires at most
comparisons. This number grows extraordinarily slowly compared to the size of the data.
Binary search does not physically move or copy data. It maintains two index pointers,

After each comparison, one boundary moves toward the other, shrinking the search space:

If target > arr[mid]: low = mid + 1    (discard left half)
If target < arr[mid]: high = mid - 1   (discard right half)
If target == arr[mid]: return mid      (found)

A critical and commonly overlooked detail: the formula for computing the middle index.

This computes the same middle index but avoids overflow by subtracting first, keeping the intermediate values small.

codes.Python:
# Dangerous (overflow risk in languages with fixed-size integers)

# Safe (no overflow risk)

content.text: In Python, integers have unlimited precision and never overflow, so both formulas are safe in Python. In Java, C, C++, and JavaScript (for very large values), always use the safe formula.
Binary search has exactly two requirements. If either is violated, the algorithm will produce incorrect results.
Requirement 1: The Data Must Be Sorted
Binary search works by comparing the target to the middle element and deciding which half to search. This logic only works if the data is ordered.

# Sorted: binary search works correctly
sorted_arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]

# Unsorted: binary search gives wrong results
unsorted_arr = [56, 2, 91, 5, 38, 23, 8, 16, 72, 12]
# Binary search on unsorted_arr will NOT reliably find values
If your data is not sorted, you must either sort it first (adding O(n log n) time) or use linear search instead.

Binary search must be able to jump directly to the middle element. This requires O(1) index access. Arrays (and Python lists) support this. Linked lists do not: finding the middle of a linked list requires traversing from the head, which takes O(n) time and destroys binary search’s efficiency.

codes.Python:
# Array / list: O(1) index access. Binary search is efficient.

print(arr[2])   # 8: instant access

# Linked list: O(n) access to reach middle. Binary search is inefficient.
# Would need to traverse node by node to find the middle

The Binary Search Algorithm Step by Step

Algorithm binary_search(arr, target):
    Set low = 0
    Set high = length(arr) - 1

    While low <= high:
        Set mid = low + (high - low) / 2

        If arr[mid] == target:
            Return mid          // Found: return the index

        If arr[mid] < target:
            Set low = mid + 1   // Target is in the right half

        If arr[mid] > target:
            Set high = mid - 1  // Target is in the left half

    Return -1                   // Not found

Initial state: low = 0, high = 9

Step 1:
  mid = 0 + (9 - 0) / 2 = 4
  arr[4] = 16
  16 < 23 → target is in right half
  low = 5

Step 2:
  mid = 5 + (9 - 5) / 2 = 7
  arr[7] = 56
  56 > 23 → target is in left half
  high = 6

Step 3:
  mid = 5 + (6 - 5) / 2 = 5
  arr[5] = 23
  23 == 23 → FOUND at index 5

Return 5

  binary_search_recursive(arr, 23, 5, 9)
    mid = 7, arr[7] = 56 > 23 → search left
    binary_search_recursive(arr, 23, 5, 6)

The iterative version uses O(1) space (no call stack). The recursive version uses O(log n) space for the call stack. In terms of time complexity, both are O(log n). For most production use cases, the iterative version is preferred because it avoids any risk of stack overflow and uses less memory.

Comparison: Binary Search vs Linear Search

The standard binary search finds any occurrence of the target. But real problems often require more: find the first occurrence, the last occurrence, or the insertion point. These variations adjust the termination condition.
When duplicates exist, the standard binary search might return any matching index. To find the leftmost (first) occurrence:

codes.Python:
def count_occurrences(arr, target):
    first = find_first(arr, target)
    if first == -1:
        return 0
    last = find_last(arr, target)
    return last - first + 1

arr = [2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 8, 10]
print(count_occurrences(arr, 4))   # 3
print(count_occurrences(arr, 5))   # 0

import bisect

arr = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
print(bisect.bisect_left(arr, 5))    # 2: lower bound
print(bisect.bisect_right(arr, 4))   # 2: upper bound (insert after last 4)

content.text: In an array that first increases then decreases (bitonic), binary search can find the peak element (the maximum).
Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
A sorted array that has been rotated (e.g.,
) can still be searched in O(log n) using modified binary search.

codes.Python:
def binary_search(arr, target):
    low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target: low = mid + 1
        else: high = mid - 1
    return -1

arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]
print(binary_search(arr, 91))   # 9 (checks 4 elements)

content.text: If you are searching a sorted array more than once, binary search is almost always the right choice. If the data is unsorted and the dataset is small, linear search is simpler. If the data is unsorted and large, consider sorting it first (O(n log n)) and then using binary search for subsequent queries, since the total cost of sort plus multiple binary searches beats repeated linear scans.

codes.Python:
import bisect

arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]

# Find insertion point (lower bound): leftmost position for target
idx = bisect.bisect_left(arr, 23)
print(idx)   # 5

# Check if element exists
if idx < len(arr) and arr[idx] == 23:
    print(f"Found 23 at index{idx}")   # Found 23 at index 5

# Find insertion point (upper bound): rightmost position
idx_right = bisect.bisect_right(arr, 23)
print(idx_right)   # 6

# Insert while maintaining sorted order
bisect.insort(arr, 25)
print(arr)   # [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 25, 38, 56, 72, 91]

content.text: Binary search is not just a way to find elements in arrays. It is embedded in some of the most important systems in computing.
Databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL store index data in

, which are balanced tree structures built on binary search principles. Every lookup in an indexed database column performs a binary search through the tree. For a table with 100 million rows, the index allows finding any record in roughly 27 comparisons instead of scanning 100 million rows.
Git Bisect: Bug Isolation in Version Control
is a tool built entirely on binary search. When you know a bug was introduced somewhere in a range of commits,

checks the commit at the midpoint, you mark it as “good” or “bad”, and it eliminates half the commits. This finds the exact commit that introduced a bug in O(log n) steps instead of checking every commit linearly.

# Imagine 1024 commits between the last known good version and the current buggy version
# git bisect finds the bad commit in at most 10 steps (log₂(1024) = 10)
git bisect start
git bisect bad                  # Current commit is bad
git bisect good v1.0            # v1.0 was good
# git bisect automatically checks the midpoint commit
# You test and mark: git bisect good / git bisect bad
# Repeats until the first bad commit is isolated

When your internet router decides where to send a data packet, it looks up the destination IP address in a routing table. Routing tables are sorted by IP address prefix, and binary search (or more advanced structures based on it) finds the correct routing entry in O(log n) time, enabling routers to forward millions of packets per second.
When you type in a search bar and suggestions appear, the system searches a sorted dictionary of terms using binary search to find all terms that start with your typed prefix. The
variation finds where the prefix starts in the sorted list, and suggestions are read from that point forward.

codes.Python:
def autocomplete(words, prefix):
    # Find the first word that starts with prefix
    low, high = 0, len(words)
    while low < high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2
        if words[mid] < prefix:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid

    suggestions = []
    i = low
    while i < len(words) and words[i].startswith(prefix):
        suggestions.append(words[i])
        i += 1

    return suggestions

words = ["apple", "application", "apply", "apt", "banana", "band", "bandana"]
print(autocomplete(words, "app"))    # ['apple', 'application', 'apply']
print(autocomplete(words, "ban"))    # ['banana', 'band', 'bandana']

causes overflow in C, Java, and other fixed-width integer languages for large arrays, which is a non-obvious but critical bug

Binary search is one of those algorithms where understanding the underlying principle, that each comparison eliminates exactly half the remaining possibilities, unlocks a way of thinking that extends far beyond array lookups. Once you see the logarithmic elimination of possibilities as a general idea, you will find binary search reasoning applicable in places that look nothing like a sorted array at first glance.

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand If Statements

Imagine you are at a traffic light. If the light is green, you drive. If it is red, you stop. If it is yellow, you slow down. You do not apply the same action regardless of what colour the light shows. You observe a condition, evaluate it, and choose a different action based on the result.

Every meaningful program in existence does exactly this. A banking app checks if your balance is sufficient before processing a withdrawal. A login system checks if your password matches before granting access. A weather app checks if the temperature is below zero before suggesting a jacket. A game checks if your health has reached zero before displaying “Game Over.”

Without the ability to make decisions based on conditions, every program would run the exact same steps in the exact same order every single time, regardless of any input. It would be a fixed recipe with no capacity to adapt. The if statement is what gives programs the ability to think, choose, and respond to the world.

The if statement is the very first and most fundamental control structure in programming. It is the building block of all decision-making logic. Loops, functions, and entire algorithms all depend on if statements to direct their behaviour. You cannot write a meaningful program without them.
Yet most beginners learn the basic syntax and stop there. They know how to write

but do not understand how conditions are evaluated at the machine level, how to combine conditions correctly without introducing bugs, when to use a chain of elif instead of nested ifs, or how short-circuit evaluation can prevent crashes and improve performance.

This blog fixes that. We will go from the very basics all the way to how boolean evaluation works under the hood, every form of the if statement, how logical and comparison operators interact, the common mistakes that cause silent bugs, and the advanced patterns that make decision logic clean, readable, and correct.
is a programming construct that executes a block of code only if a specified condition evaluates to
, the block is skipped entirely and the program continues with whatever comes after.
The if statement is a built-in feature of every programming language, not something you build yourself
One or many lines of code are grouped together and treated as a unit
Only if a condition is true:
The code inside the block runs zero times (if the condition is false) or once (if it is true)
The program does not crash or pause. It simply jumps past the block and continues normally
Without an if statement, code runs unconditionally:

codes.Python:
temperature = 15
print("It is cold outside.")   # Always prints, regardless of temperature
print("Wear a coat.")          # Always prints, regardless of temperature

content.text: With an if statement, code runs only when the condition is met:

codes.Python:
temperature = 15

if temperature < 20:
    print("It is cold outside.")   # Prints only when temperature < 20
    print("Wear a coat.")          # Prints only when temperature < 20

content.text: How If Statements Work Under the Hood
This is the section most tutorials skip, and it explains what is actually happening inside the processor when an if statement runs.
Every condition inside an if statement evaluates to a
(0). The processor does not think in words like “greater than” or “equal to.” It performs arithmetic comparisons and produces a single bit: 1 for true and 0 for false.

codes.Python:
x = 5

print(x > 3)    # True  (boolean result of the comparison)
print(x > 10)   # False
print(x == 5)   # True
print(type(x > 3))   # <class 'bool'>

content.text: Jump Instructions at the CPU Level
When your program runs, the if statement compiles down to a

at the machine code level. The CPU evaluates the condition and sets a flag in its status register. The conditional jump instruction checks that flag and either continues to the next instruction (if the condition is true and the block should execute) or jumps forward past the block (if the condition is false).

; Simplified machine code for: if (x > 5) { do_something(); }
LOAD x into register A
COMPARE A with 5
SET condition flag (1 if greater, 0 if not)
JUMP_IF_FALSE to label_skip     ; Skip the block if condition is false
CALL do_something               ; This runs only if condition was true
label_skip:
CONTINUE...                     ; Program resumes here regardless
This is why if statements have essentially zero overhead: they translate to a single comparison and a single jump instruction, which the CPU executes in one clock cycle.
In many languages, the condition in an if statement does not have to be an explicit boolean. The language evaluates any value for its
: whether it behaves as true or false in a boolean context.

codes.Python:
# Falsy values in Python (evaluate as False in an if condition)
if 0:       print("This never runs")    # 0 is falsy
if "":      print("This never runs")    # Empty string is falsy
if []:      print("This never runs")    # Empty list is falsy
if None:    print("This never runs")    # None is falsy

# Truthy values (evaluate as True in an if condition)
if 1:           print("Runs")    # Any non-zero number is truthy
if "hello":     print("Runs")    # Non-empty string is truthy
if [1, 2, 3]:   print("Runs")    # Non-empty list is truthy
if -99:         print("Runs")    # Negative numbers are truthy too

If statements are the decision-making engine behind every application you use. Here are the specific places where they power real systems.
Every login page uses if statements to verify credentials and grant or deny access.

stored_password = "secure123"
max_attempts = 3
attempts = 0

def login(username, password):
    global attempts
    attempts += 1

    if attempts > max_attempts:
        print("Account locked due to too many failed attempts.")
        return

    if username == "" or password == "":
        print("Username and password cannot be empty.")
        return

    if password == stored_password:
        print(f"Welcome,{username}! Login successful.")
        attempts = 0
    else:
        remaining = max_attempts - attempts

The if statement appears at first glance to be a trivially simple concept, but it is the foundation of all decision-making logic in programming.

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand Comments
Imagine you wrote a complex piece of code six months ago. You open it today and see a function with variable names like
, and a loop with three nested conditions. You cannot remember what any of it does. You spend an hour reverse-engineering your own work just to understand it enough to make a small change.

Now imagine you had added two lines of comments when you wrote it. “This function calculates the shortest delivery route between two warehouse locations using Dijkstra’s algorithm.” Suddenly, you know exactly what you are looking at, why you wrote it that way, and what you need to change. Five minutes instead of an hour.
That is the difference comments make. But the value goes far beyond reminding yourself what your own code does.

Think about a team of ten developers building a payment system together. Without comments, every developer has to read every line of every file they touch to understand what it does before they can safely modify it. With clear comments, the intent of each function is stated in plain language. New team members onboard in days instead of weeks. Code reviews become faster. Bugs get caught earlier because the reviewer can immediately see whether the code matches its stated purpose.

Comments are not just annotations. They are the documentation that keeps software alive and maintainable over time. The software that powers banks, hospitals, aircraft, and infrastructure is maintained by teams of developers who change over years. The only thing connecting the code written today to the developer who will modify it five years from now is documentation, and in-code documentation means comments.

Yet most beginners treat comments as an afterthought. They write no comments while coding, then add a few vague notes at the end, or write comments that simply restate what the code already says. They do not understand the different types of comments, how to write ones that genuinely help, or how over-commenting can be just as harmful as under-commenting.

This blog fixes that. We will go from the very basics all the way to how compilers process comments, every type of comment and when each is appropriate, the professional conventions used in industry, and the practices that separate comments which genuinely help from comments that create noise.
is a piece of text written inside source code that is completely ignored by the compiler or interpreter. It is intended entirely for human readers, not for the machine.
Comments can be a single word, a full sentence, a paragraph, or even a diagram made of characters
Comments live directly in the code file, right alongside the code they describe
The program runs exactly as if the comment were not there. Comments have zero effect on program behaviour
The audience is the developer reading the code, not the machine executing it
Without comments, code is often hard to understand at a glance:

codes.Python:
def calc(p, r, t):
    return p * (1 + r/100) ** t

content.text: With comments, the purpose and parameters are immediately clear:

codes.Python:
# Calculate compound interest
# p = principal amount, r = annual interest rate (%), t = time in years
def calc(p, r, t):
    return p * (1 + r/100) ** t

content.text: The two functions produce identical output. The difference is entirely in how quickly a human can understand and safely modify the second one.

content.text: How Comments Work Under the Hood
This is the section most tutorials skip, and it explains what actually happens to your comments when the code runs.
When you run or compile a program, the source code goes through several stages before it becomes executable instructions. Comments are handled in the very first stage:

Source code (.py / .js / .java / .c)
        |
        v
  LEXICAL ANALYSER (Scanner)
  - Reads characters one by one
  - Identifies tokens: keywords, operators, identifiers, literals
  - STRIPS COMMENTS COMPLETELY at this stage
        |
        v
  Token stream (no comments)
        |
        v
  Parser → Compiler/Interpreter → Executable
The lexical analyser (the first phase of the compiler or interpreter) reads your source file character by character. When it encounters the start of a comment (
), it reads forward until it finds the end of the comment and then discards everything between those markers entirely. The rest of the compilation pipeline never sees the comment text at all.
Because comments are removed before any execution or compilation happens, they have:
A file with 10,000 lines of comments runs at exactly the same speed as the same file with no comments
Zero impact on binary size (compiled languages):
in C) contains no trace of your comments
Slight impact on source file size and load time (interpreted languages):
file from disk and must scan past comments. For files with extremely large comment blocks, this has a theoretically measurable but practically negligible effect

Comments are completely free from a performance perspective. There is no technical reason to avoid writing thorough comments. The only cost of a comment is the time it takes you to write it, and that cost is always outweighed by the time it saves every person who reads the code afterward, including yourself six months later.
How the Tokeniser Handles Comment Delimiters
The tokeniser uses a simple state machine to detect and discard comments.

Read character
If character is '/' and next character is '/':
    Discard all characters until end of line
    Return to normal reading

Read character
If character is '/' and next character is '*':
    Enter comment mode
    Discard all characters until you see '*' followed by '/'
    Return to normal reading
This is why nested multi-line comments do not work in C or Java. The tokeniser stops at the first
it finds, regardless of how many
Comments are categorised by their format, their span, and their purpose. Understanding each type helps you choose the right one for each situation.
starts with a specific symbol and continues until the end of that line. Everything from the symbol to the newline character is ignored.

# This is a single-line comment
# The function below checks if a number is prime

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:        # Numbers less than 2 are not prime
        return False
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):   # Only check up to square root
        if n % i == 0:
            return False   # Found a factor: not prime
    return True

def calculate_compound_interest(principal, rate, times_compounded, years):
    """
    Calculate the compound interest earned over a period.

    Uses the formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)

    Args:
        principal (float): The initial amount of money. Must be positive.
        rate (float): Annual interest rate as a decimal (e.g., 0.05 for 5%).
        times_compounded (int): Number of times interest compounds per year.
        years (float): Number of years the money is invested.

    Returns:
        float: Total amount after compound interest is applied.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If principal or rate is negative.

    Example:
        >>> calculate_compound_interest(1000, 0.05, 12, 5)
        1283.35
    """
    if principal < 0 or rate < 0:
        raise ValueError("Principal and rate must be non-negative")
    return principal * (1 + rate / times_compounded) ** (times_compounded * years)

content.text: Comments are not optional in professional software development. Here are the specific ways they keep real systems working.
Open Source Libraries: Helping Thousands of Developers

Every popular library (NumPy, React, Spring, the Linux kernel) relies on comments to enable contributions from developers around the world who did not write the original code. Without comments, a contributor would need to read thousands of lines of unfamiliar code to understand the intent of every function before making even a small change.

def convolve(a, b, mode='full', method='auto'):

content.text: Write Comments for the Next Reader

Always write comments as if the next reader has never seen this code before. That reader might be a new team member, a contractor, a future maintainer, or yourself six months from now when you have forgotten the details.

codes.Python:
# Bad: assumes the reader knows the context
# Update the flag
user.is_verified = True

# Good: explains why this is happening here, not just what
# Mark user as verified after successful email confirmation
# This unlocks their ability to post content and make purchases
user.is_verified = True

content.text: The code already shows what is happening. Comments should explain why it was written this way, what the intent is, and what a reader needs to understand to safely modify it.

codes.Python:
# Bad: just restates the code
result = x * 0.9   # Multiply x by 0.9

# Good: explains the business reason
result = x * 0.9   # Apply 10% loyalty discount for members with over 1 year tenure

codes.Python:
# Bad: complex algorithm with zero explanation
def kmp_search(text, pattern):
    m, n = len(pattern), len(text)
    fail = [0] * m
    j = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        while j > 0 and pattern[i] != pattern[j]:
            j = fail[j - 1]
        if pattern[i] == pattern[j]:
            j += 1
        fail[i] = j
    # ...

# Good: explain the algorithm and the non-obvious data structure
def kmp_search(text, pattern):
    """
    Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search: O(n + m) time.

    Uses a failure function (fail[]) to avoid re-examining characters
    in text after a partial match fails. fail[i] is the length of the
    longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix.
    """
    m, n = len(pattern), len(text)
    fail = [0] * m   # Failure function: precomputed prefix-suffix lengths
    j = 0            # Length of current matching prefix
    for i in range(1, m):
        while j > 0 and pattern[i] != pattern[j]:
            j = fail[j - 1]   # Fall back to longest viable prefix
        if pattern[i] == pattern[j]:
            j += 1
        fail[i] = j

content.text: Well-written comments let any developer understand the intent of a block of code without having to reverse-engineer it from the logic alone, dramatically reducing the time to understand unfamiliar code

Comments allow multiple developers to work on the same codebase efficiently. Each function or module explains its contract, which means developers can use code they did not write without needing to read all of its implementation
Documentation comments (docstrings, Javadoc, JSDoc) allow tools to automatically generate API documentation websites, IDE tooltips, and developer guides from the source code itself

When a bug is reported in production, comments that explain the intended behaviour help developers quickly determine whether the code is doing what it was supposed to do, or whether the intention was wrong
Complex business rules, regulatory requirements, and non-obvious decisions often need to be preserved alongside the code that implements them. Comments are the natural place for this
Reviewers can check whether the code matches its stated intention in the comments, catching logic errors that would be invisible if they could only see the code
A comment that no longer describes the current behaviour misleads readers into thinking the code does something it does not. This can cause developers to make incorrect assumptions and introduce bugs

Too many comments, especially ones that restate what the code already says clearly, make it harder to spot the comments that carry real information. Readers learn to skim all comments, including important ones
Comments can mask poor code quality:

Writing a comment to explain a confusing piece of code is sometimes used as a substitute for writing cleaner code. A better approach is usually to refactor the code to be self-explanatory, and then add a brief comment only for the genuinely non-obvious parts

Comments are source code. If your repository is ever accidentally made public, or if a developer copies code, any credentials, API keys, personal data, or security notes in comments are exposed alongside the code
Different languages have completely different comment syntaxes. A developer who works in multiple languages must remember
, and can accidentally write the wrong style, which may be silently treated as code rather than a comment
Unlike code, there is nothing in the toolchain that checks whether a comment accurately describes the function it accompanies. Stale comments can persist for years without anyone noticing
Comments seem like a trivial topic at first glance, but they are the primary tool that keeps software understandable and maintainable over time.
Here is a recap of everything covered:
A comment is a piece of text in source code that is
completely ignored by the compiler or interpreter
and is intended entirely for human readers
At the compiler level, comments are stripped by the
in the very first stage of compilation. They have zero effect on the compiled output, binary size, or runtime performance
) are for brief explanations of specific lines or small code blocks.
) are for describing modules, classes, and complex algorithms

(docstrings in Python, Javadoc in Java, JSDoc in JavaScript) use a special format that allows tools to automatically generate API documentation, IDE tooltips, and developer guides from the source code
explain the why behind a specific line. They should not restate what the code clearly says, they should add information the code cannot express by itself
temporarily disables lines for debugging or comparison. Long-term commented-out code should be deleted because version control preserves the history
open source collaboration, safety-critical systems, database migration records, algorithm explanations
. The code shows what is happening. The comment explains the business reason, the edge case, the formula, or the decision that cannot be expressed in code alone

Comments are a conversation between the developer who wrote the code and every developer who will ever read it. The quality of that conversation determines whether your code is a helpful contribution to the people who use it or a puzzle that takes hours to decode. Write for the next reader, explain the non-obvious, keep comments accurate, and your code will serve its purpose long after you have moved on to the next project.

title: What is Stack in Data Structure ?

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand the Stack

Every time you press Ctrl+Z in a text editor, something invisible happens in the background. The program does not scan through the entire document to figure out what you last did. It does not search any list or database. It goes directly to a structure that remembers the most recent action and undoes it instantly. That structure is a stack.

Now think about how your computer runs any program at all. Every time a function calls another function, which calls another function, the computer needs to remember where to return when each one finishes. When
, the computer must remember to return from
, in that exact reverse order. The mechanism that makes this possible is called the call stack. It is a stack data structure running at the hardware level of every program ever written.

Think bigger. Every web browser you use has a forward and backward navigation system. Every compiler checks that your parentheses and braces are balanced before running your code. Every calculator evaluates
in the correct order. Every depth-first graph search explores nodes systematically. Every one of these features depends on a stack.

The stack is one of the most fundamental and frequently used data structures in all of computer science. It is elegant in its simplicity: you can only add or remove from one end, the top. This single constraint turns out to be exactly what dozens of real problems need.

Yet most beginners learn the basic LIFO definition and the two operations push and pop, then move on. They do not understand how a stack is stored in memory, why array-based and linked-list-based implementations have different trade-offs, how the call stack works at the CPU level, or how problems that look nothing like a stack can be solved beautifully using one.

This blog fixes that. We will go from the very basics all the way to how a stack is laid out in memory, every core operation with full implementations in four languages, both implementation approaches with their trade-offs, and the advanced patterns that make the stack one of the most versatile tools in a programmer’s toolkit.

content.text: How a Stack Works Under the Hood
This is the section most tutorials skip, and it explains what is actually happening in memory when you push and pop elements.
When a stack is implemented using an
, all elements are stored in consecutive memory addresses. The stack maintains a single integer variable called
that records the index of the topmost element. Initially,
by 1, write the new value at
The data at the old position is not erased immediately (it is “dead” data), but it will be overwritten by the next push. The
pointer is the only mechanism that determines what is “in” the stack.
The Call Stack: A Stack Running in Your CPU
The most important stack in computing is the
, which your operating system and CPU maintain automatically for every running program. Every time a function is called, the CPU pushes a
onto the call stack. This frame contains:
The return address (where to go back to when the function finishes)

Program running main():

main() calls login()
  PUSH frame: login()
  login() calls validatePassword()
    PUSH frame: validatePassword()
    validatePassword() returns → POP frame
  login() continues
  login() returns → POP frame
main() continues
The call stack ensures functions return in the correct reverse order. This is exactly LIFO: the most recently called function must finish first before control returns to its caller.
Two error conditions are unique to stacks:
Attempting to push an element onto a full stack (when using a fixed-size array implementation).
Attempting to pop an element from an empty stack.

The term “stack overflow” in the error message you may have seen in programs, and the name of the famous Q&A website, comes directly from this data structure. When a program recurses too deeply, the call stack literally overflows its allocated memory, causing the program to crash.
is the rule that governs every stack operation. It is not just a definition to memorise. It is the fundamental property that makes stacks useful for a specific category of problems.

After push(A):   [A]             top → A
After push(B):   [A, B]          top → B
After push(C):   [A, B, C]       top → C
After push(D):   [A, B, C, D]    top → D

pop() returns D  →  Stack: [A, B, C]    top → C
pop() returns C  →  Stack: [A, B]       top → B
pop() returns B  →  Stack: [A]          top → A
pop() returns A  →  Stack: []           (empty)
: exactly the reverse of the input order
. This reversal property is one of the most powerful things a stack can do.
The LIFO property means a stack is the natural tool for any problem that requires:
Processing things in the opposite order they arrived
Returning to a previous state when the current path fails
Handling a structure where inner items must be resolved before outer ones (like function calls, or matched parentheses)
Remembering recent actions in reverse chronological order (like undo)
Every stack implementation provides five fundamental operations. Understanding each one clearly is the foundation for using stacks correctly.
Remove and return the top element
Return the top element without removing it
Return true if the stack has no elements
Return true if the stack is at max capacity (array-based)
All five operations are O(1): they take constant time regardless of how many elements are in the stack. This is the defining performance characteristic of a well-implemented stack.
operation adds a new element to the top of the stack. Before pushing, it checks if the stack is full (for fixed-size implementations).

push(value):
  1. Check if stack is full
  2. If full → print "Stack Overflow" and stop
  3. If not full → increment top pointer by 1
  4. Store value at stack[top]
  5. Return success

codes.Python:
class Stack:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.stack = []
        self.capacity = capacity

    def push(self, element):
        if len(self.stack) == self.capacity:
            print("Stack Overflow: stack is full")
            return
        self.stack.append(element)
        print(f"Pushed:{element}")

s = Stack(5)
s.push(44)    # Pushed: 44
s.push(10)    # Pushed: 10
s.push(62)    # Pushed: 62
print(s.stack)  # [44, 10, 62]

pop():
  1. Check if stack is empty
  2. If empty → print "Stack Underflow" and stop
  3. If not empty → store value at stack[top] in a variable
  4. Decrement top pointer by 1
  5. Return the stored value

def pop(self):
    if len(self.stack) == 0:
        print("Stack Underflow: stack is empty")
        return None
    element = self.stack.pop()
    print(f"Popped:{element}")
    return element

# Using the Stack class from above
s = Stack(5)
s.push(44)
s.push(10)
s.push(62)
print(s.stack)    # [44, 10, 62]

s.pop()           # Popped: 62
s.pop()           # Popped: 10
print(s.stack)    # [44]

content.text: In a fixed-size implementation, when the array fills up and pops clear some space, those freed positions cannot normally be reused. A circular stack wraps the array so that empty positions at the beginning are reused after elements at the end are popped. Used when memory is constrained and elements flow continuously in and out.

Positions: [0] [1] [2] [3] [4]
                             ^-- When full, next push wraps to [0] if it is empty
An array-based stack stores all elements in a contiguous block of memory. The
variable is an index into the array.
Memory-efficient: no extra pointer storage per element
Fast: cache-friendly because elements are contiguous in memory
Fixed size: must know the maximum capacity in advance
A linked-list-based stack stores each element in a separate node. Each node contains the data and a pointer to the node below it. The top of the stack is the head of the linked list.
Dynamic size: grows and shrinks on demand, no maximum
No overflow (except due to total memory exhaustion)
Extra memory per element (each node stores a pointer)
Not cache-friendly (nodes are scattered in memory)
Array vs Linked List for Stack Implementation
Time Complexity of All Stack Operations
All primary stack operations are O(1). The only exception is search, which requires scanning all elements.
O(n) where n is the capacity
O(n) where n is the number of elements currently stored
O(d) where d is the recursion depth
Stacks and queues are frequently taught together because they are structurally similar (both linear, both access-restricted) but fundamentally opposite in their ordering principle.

content.text: The stack is one of the most widely used data structures in computer science. Here are the specific real systems that depend on it every day.
Function Call Management: The Call Stack
Every programming language runtime uses a stack to manage function calls. When
, the return addresses and local variables of each function are pushed onto the call stack. They are popped off in reverse order as each function completes.

codes.Python:
def function_c():
    print("Inside C")
    # Stack at this point: [main → A → B → C]

def function_b():
    print("Inside B")
    function_c()   # Push C onto the call stack
    print("Back in B")  # After C pops, execution returns here

def function_a():
    print("Inside A")
    function_b()   # Push B onto the call stack
    print("Back in A")  # After B pops, execution returns here

function_a()
# Output:
# Inside A
# Inside B
# Inside C
# Back in B
# Back in A

content.text: Every text editor implements Ctrl+Z (undo) and Ctrl+Y (redo) using two stacks. The undo stack records every action performed. The redo stack holds actions that were undone and can be reapplied.

codes.Python:
class TextEditor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.text = ""
        self.undo_stack = []   # Records actions for undoing
        self.redo_stack = []   # Records actions for redoing

    def type(self, characters):
        self.undo_stack.append(("type", characters))
        self.redo_stack.clear()   # New action clears redo history
        self.text += characters
        print(f"Text: '{self.text}'")

    def undo(self):
        if not self.undo_stack:
            print("Nothing to undo")
            return
        action, data = self.undo_stack.pop()   # Get last action
        self.redo_stack.append((action, data))  # Save for redo
        if action == "type":
            self.text = self.text[:-len(data)]   # Remove typed characters
        print(f"Undo → Text: '{self.text}'")

    def redo(self):
        if not self.redo_stack:
            print("Nothing to redo")
            return
        action, data = self.redo_stack.pop()
        self.undo_stack.append((action, data))
        if action == "type":
            self.text += data
        print(f"Redo → Text: '{self.text}'")

editor = TextEditor()
editor.type("Hello")      # Text: 'Hello'
editor.type(" World")     # Text: 'Hello World'
editor.undo()             # Undo → Text: 'Hello'
editor.undo()             # Undo → Text: ''
editor.redo()             # Redo → Text: 'Hello'

content.text: Every compiler uses a stack to check that opening brackets, braces, and parentheses are properly matched and closed in the correct order. This is one of the classic stack problems.

codes.Python:
def is_balanced(expression):
    stack = []
    opening = set("([{")
    closing = set(")]}")
    matches = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}

    for char in expression:
        if char in opening:
            stack.append(char)         # Push every opening bracket
        elif char in closing:
            if not stack:              # No matching opening bracket
                return False
            if stack[-1] != matches[char]:   # Mismatched bracket type
                return False
            stack.pop()                # Matched: remove from stack

    return len(stack) == 0   # Stack must be empty if all brackets matched

print(is_balanced("({[]})"))   # True
print(is_balanced("([)]"))     # False: wrong nesting order
print(is_balanced("{[}"))      # False: unclosed bracket
print(is_balanced("((()))"))   # True

content.text: Web browsers use two stacks to implement navigation history. Every URL you visit is pushed onto the back stack. Pressing back pops from the back stack. Pressing forward pops from the forward stack.

codes.Python:
class Browser:
    def __init__(self):
        self.back_stack = []
        self.forward_stack = []
        self.current_url = "about:blank"

    def visit(self, url):
        self.back_stack.append(self.current_url)
        self.forward_stack.clear()   # New visit clears forward history
        self.current_url = url
        print(f"Visiting:{self.current_url}")

    def back(self):
        if not self.back_stack:
            print("Cannot go back: no history")
            return
        self.forward_stack.append(self.current_url)
        self.current_url = self.back_stack.pop()
        print(f"Back:{self.current_url}")

    def forward(self):
        if not self.forward_stack:
            print("Cannot go forward")
            return
        self.back_stack.append(self.current_url)
        self.current_url = self.forward_stack.pop()
        print(f"Forward:{self.current_url}")

browser = Browser()
browser.visit("google.com")      # Visiting: google.com
browser.visit("github.com")      # Visiting: github.com
browser.visit("stackoverflow.com")  # Visiting: stackoverflow.com
browser.back()                   # Back: github.com
browser.back()                   # Back: google.com
browser.forward()                # Forward: github.com

content.text: Calculators and compilers evaluate expressions like
using a stack. The expression is first converted to
(also called Reverse Polish Notation), which is then evaluated using a stack.

codes.Python:
def evaluate_postfix(expression):
    """
    Evaluate a postfix expression like "3 4 2 * +" (equals 3 + 4*2 = 11).
    Numbers are pushed onto the stack.
    Operators pop two numbers, compute the result, and push it back.
    """
    stack = []
    tokens = expression.split()

    for token in tokens:
        if token.lstrip('-').isdigit():   # It is a number
            stack.append(int(token))
        else:                              # It is an operator
            b = stack.pop()               # Second operand
            a = stack.pop()               # First operand
            if token == '+': stack.append(a + b)
            elif token == '-': stack.append(a - b)
            elif token == '*': stack.append(a * b)
            elif token == '/': stack.append(a // b)

    return stack[0]   # Final result is the only remaining element

print(evaluate_postfix("3 4 2 * +"))    # 11  (3 + 4*2)
print(evaluate_postfix("5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -"))  # 14

content.text: Depth-first search (DFS) explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking. It naturally uses a stack: push neighbours to explore, pop to visit, push their neighbours, and so on.
Using Two Stacks to Implement a Queue

Two stacks can simulate a queue’s FIFO behaviour. Elements are pushed onto the input stack. When dequeuing, if the output stack is empty, all elements from the input stack are transferred (reversing their order).
Finding the Minimum Element in O(1)
By maintaining a second “min stack” that tracks the minimum at each level, you can get the current minimum in O(1) time.
Reversing a String Using a Stack
The natural reversal property of a stack makes reversing a string trivially elegant.

codes.Python:
def reverse_string(s):
    stack = list(s)   # Push all characters onto the stack
    result = ""
    while stack:
        result += stack.pop()   # Pop reverses the order
    return result

print(reverse_string("hello"))     # "olleh"
print(reverse_string("Stack!"))    # "!kcatS"

content.text: You can sort a stack using only one additional stack and the standard push/pop/peek operations.

codes.Python:
def sort_stack(stack):
    sorted_stack = []

    while stack:
        temp = stack.pop()   # Take the top element

        # Move elements from sorted_stack back to stack until correct position
        while sorted_stack and sorted_stack[-1] > temp:
            stack.append(sorted_stack.pop())

        sorted_stack.append(temp)   # Place temp in its correct position

    return sorted_stack

stack = [34, 3, 31, 98, 92, 23]
print(sort_stack(stack))   # [3, 23, 31, 34, 92, 98]

content.text: Push, pop, and peek all run in constant time regardless of the number of elements in the stack. This makes stacks extremely efficient for any problem that only needs to access the top element
Both array-based and linked-list-based implementations require minimal code. The logic is straightforward and easy to reason about
Elements are stored compactly with no extra pointer overhead. The only overhead is a single integer tracking the top position
Any problem involving reversal, backtracking, nesting, or maintaining a history of recent operations maps directly onto a stack’s behaviour with no algorithmic complexity
The call stack, expression evaluation, syntax checking, and undo systems all depend on stacks. Understanding stacks means understanding how these systems work at their core
Any recursive algorithm can be converted to an iterative one by explicitly managing a stack, allowing you to avoid stack overflow for deeply recursive problems
You can only directly access the top element. Reaching any other element requires popping all elements above it, which takes O(n) time and destroys the stack’s state
A statically allocated array-based stack has a maximum capacity. If you exceed it, stack overflow occurs. You must know the maximum size in advance, which is not always possible
Each node in a linked-list stack must store a pointer to the next node in addition to the data. For large numbers of small elements, this overhead can be significant
If your use case requires accessing elements by position (get the 5th element from the bottom), a stack is the wrong choice. Use an array or linked list directly
When using the call stack for deep recursion (thousands of recursive calls), the call stack can overflow. Languages like Python have a default recursion limit of 1,000 calls for this reason
The stack provides no built-in way to search for a specific element without disrupting its structure. Search requires O(n) time and destructively pops all elements until the target is found

The stack is one of the simplest and most powerful data structures in computer science. Its single constraint, access from only one end, turns out to be exactly the right property for an enormous range of important problems.
Here is a recap of everything covered:

At the memory level, an array-based stack stores elements contiguously and uses a single
pointer to track the topmost element. All operations are O(1) because they only move this pointer and read or write one memory location
Every stack needs exactly five operations:

The stack’s power comes not from complexity but from simplicity. One rule, two operations, constant time. That combination solves an astounding variety of problems that would otherwise require far more complex logic. When you encounter a problem involving reversal, nesting, backtracking, or recent history, your first instinct should be to reach for a stack.

content.text: Why Every Programmer Needs to Understand Arrays

Every list you have ever seen in a program, every leaderboard in a game, every row in a spreadsheet, every pixel in an image on your screen, every frame in a video, every contact in your phone’s address book, is stored using an array or a data structure built on top of one.

Think about how YouTube suggests videos. It maintains lists of videos ranked by relevance, lists of recently watched content, lists of trending topics, lists of search results. Every single one of those lists is managed as an array of items. Sorting them, searching through them, accessing the one you clicked on, all of these operations happen on arrays millions of times per second across YouTube’s servers.
Now think smaller. You write a program that needs to store the test scores of thirty students. You could create thirty separate variables:
. Then when you need to find the average, you write the same addition operation thirty times. When the class grows to forty students, you rewrite the entire program.

Or you store the scores in an array. One variable. Access any score in one step. Find the average by looping through one structure. Add a student by adding one element. The array makes the problem manageable, and that scalability is exactly why arrays exist.

Arrays are the most fundamental data structure in computer science. Every other data structure, stacks, queues, heaps, hash tables, graphs, is either built directly on top of arrays or conceptually compared to them. You cannot understand DSA without understanding arrays first.

Yet most beginners learn only how to create an array and access elements by index, without ever understanding how an array is stored in memory, why index access is O(1) while insertion in the middle is O(n), or how two-dimensional and multi-dimensional arrays work under the hood.

This blog fixes that. We will go from the very basics all the way to memory layout, every core operation with full implementations in four languages, time complexity analysis, static vs dynamic arrays, and the real-world systems that depend on arrays every day.

Elements are arranged in a straight sequence, one after another, on a single level
All elements in a traditional array must be of one type: all integers, all floats, all characters, or all strings
The elements are physically stored side by side in memory, with no gaps between them
Every element has a unique position number starting from 0, and you can jump directly to any position in one step
